claim: Traffic signals adapt through local reinforcement learning, where each intersection adjusts its timing based on immediate traffic flow rewards without explicit coordination.
mechanism: Each intersection controller operates as an independent agent that continuously evaluates traffic flow metrics (queue length, vehicle count) and adjusts signal timing parameters using a reward function that prioritizes minimizing local delay. Controllers share minimal information with adjacent intersections only to maintain platoon coordination.
evidence: Reinforcement learning has shown success in isolated traffic signal optimization
Emergent coordination has been observed in distributed systems
assumptions: Local optimization leads to global optimum
Intersections have sufficient computational capacity for continuous learning
Traffic patterns exhibit sufficient regularity for reinforcement learning to converge
expected_failure_modes: Suboptimal global performance due to local optimization conflicts
Computational overload at intersection controllers during high-traffic periods
novelty_rationale: Applies a reinforcement learning framework to traffic signal adaptation, treating each intersection as an independent learning agent rather than a coordinated system.
testability: Can be tested in simulation by implementing reinforcement learning algorithms at each intersection and measuring convergence time and system-wide performance metrics.
falsifier: If the system fails to converge within the required 15-minute timeframe or exhibits oscillatory behavior when tested with varying traffic patterns, this hypothesis would be proven wrong.
